what: Neusis angle trisector. One motor sets an input angle. Two equal-radius arms, a straight baseline guide and a sliding marked line constrain the passive output. The marked distance equals the circle radius, so the line heading is one third of the input angle on the supplied branch. Compare the physical model with the marked joint one hole inward: the same program should then produce a different angular law. One motor sets an input angle. Equal circle radii and a marked sliding line make the passive line angle one third as large. Move one mark inward and compare the same finite input program.
try: Load the model, press Reset, then Run. Find the driven circle arm and the passive yellow line; only the circle input has a motor.
Predict the line headings at input angles 50°, 65°, 80° and 95° before watching the pauses: 16⅔°, 21⅔°, 26⅔° and 31⅔°. Read the line itself, not just the motor encoder.
Watch the long return and repeated forward sweep. The line should retrace the same geometric relation while both sliders stay engaged.

Load thirdline-control.ldr and run the identical program from Reset. Its marked segment is 24 mm instead of 32 mm, while the circle radius remains 32 mm. Predict whether its line angle should remain exactly one third.
Reset before every fresh run after manual movement or interruption. Keep the finite supplied sector; branch changes and full turns are outside the demonstration.
why: The two arms keep A and B on one circle. The line passes through A and B, and its other mark C stays on the baseline. The fixed marked distance BC closes the remaining geometric condition. With radius r and mark spacing d, this branch obeys sin(θ−2φ)=(d/r)sinφ. When d=r, the relevant angles give θ=3φ. Shortening d leaves the line free to move but changes the law. The third is produced by physical constraints; the output receives no calculated target.
matters: Trisecting an arbitrary angle with compass and unmarked straightedge alone is impossible; Pierre Wantzel proved this in 1837. Archimedes avoided the restriction by marking two points on his ruler and sliding it into place (a neusis construction). This model builds that sliding, marked ruler from beams and guides, so the geometry computes the third with no gear ratio and no output motor. It is an example of a mechanical computer: constraints, not code, produce the answer.
question: The input advances from 65° to 80°, a 15° step. How much should the main line turn? Does the one-hole-shorter marked segment have to give the same result?
answer: The equal-mark main should advance from 21⅔° to 26⅔°, exactly 5°. With the shorter mark, d = r no longer holds and exact trisection fails: ideally the line moves from about 23.720° to 29.251°, a 5.531° step. In the simulator the main line turned 5.005° for a measured 15.02° input step, and the shorter-mark version 5.539°.
further: Derive β=180°−θ+2φ from the chord joining the two circle points. Then use the baseline condition r sinβ=d sinφ to recover the closure law.
Compare equal 15° input target steps. The main ideal line steps are all 5°; the shorter-mark comparison steps vary slightly.
Compare Apex, whose one-third rotor motion comes from planetary gears, and Cross Ratio, whose factor of three applies to a half-angle tangent rather than the angle.
The nominal construction does not rate a physical model’s accuracy. Pin play, axle bending, guide friction and cable forces require separate hardware checks.
formula: Main: OA=OB=BC=r=32 mm; θ=3φ on the selected bounded branch. General marked length d: sin(θ−2φ)=(d/r)sinφ, equivalently θ=2φ+asin[(d/r)sinφ] on this branch. Comparison: d=24 mm, r=32 mm, d/r=0.75. θ is the measured input-arm heading and φ the measured passive line heading, using the same positive projected angular direction.
